content:
When: 26 September 2026, 09:00–12:00 (Vietnam time)
Venue: 26th floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City
Role: Attendee
Working backwards from the judging criteria The organisers opened the kickoff by explaining the challenge and what teams would need to demonstrate. That gave the icebreaker a purpose. As we talked about our AWS experience and the AI problems we wanted to try, it became easier to see which skills a team could put to use and what it could reasonably deliver in a demo.
Trying the AI agent challenge The mentor-supported exercise brought together three ideas I had mostly encountered separately. A prompt describes the task, a knowledge base supplies reference material, and retrieval-augmented generation brings relevant passages into the model’s context. It gave me a specific question to ask when an answer seems poorly supported: which passage did the application actually retrieve? Reading that passage alongside the answer helps narrow down where to make a change.
The career Q&A followed naturally from the exercise. Questions about AWS certifications and practice projects felt more concrete after spending time on a problem with other participants and mentors.
What I would use again At the start of my next team challenge, I would write down one example input and the result we want to show. The team can return to that same example when it presents the demo. For PhishGuard, I would open a suspicious-message report and show the passage from a playbook that helps an analyst interpret the result.

title: 5.1 · Problem and architecture
content:
An employee forwards a suspicious email while a colleague submits a screenshot of the same campaign. SecOps needs to preserve both originals, establish who can read each report and record the reason for a decision. This lab builds that process in US East (N. Virginia).
Open the full-resolution diagram · draw.io
How to read the diagram The browser loads React through CloudFront. Cognito issues a JWT. The HTTP API validates it for the Reporter and Admin APIs. The APIs use DynamoDB to check ownership, read incidents and record decisions. A browser uploads an image or EML directly to S3 using a presigned POST returned by the Reporter API. For pasted text or a demo fixture the Reporter API writes/copies the object. All three web paths produce uploads/{uuid}/raw. An S3 ObjectCreated notification calls Ingest. SES uses a separate receipt rule: store the original MIME in inbound/, then invoke Ingest with receipt verdicts. Ingest validates, computes SHA-256 and saves the raw object in the evidence bucket with versioning, SSE-KMS and seven-day Governance retention. After the save it starts the execution named for the incident, passing evidence references including raw_s3_key, raw_s3_version_id when available, and evidence_sha256. The sanitized bucket holds a separate redacted analysis copy. The SQS dead-letter queue receives failed async Ingest deliveries. Extract & Redact reads the evidence, runs Vietnamese/English Tesseract for images, and masks detectable PII. Insufficient usable text and QR evidence leads to NEEDS_MORE_INFO. Triage scores rules and checks indicators. Synthesize retrieves playbook passages and requests a Bedrock summary when configured. A deterministic fallback stays visible when synthesis fails. A high/critical report without a valid action goes to NEEDS_REVIEW with an SNS notice. A lower-risk report without a proposal ends at NO_ACTION. With a valid proposal, PrepareApproval persists the token and PENDING_APPROVAL before notifying SecOps. The Standard workflow holds the wait. The Lambda invocation returns. An admin reads the proposal and submits a decision. Admin API checks state and role, then calls SendTaskSuccess with the decision. Rejection ends at REJECTED. Expiry follows the timeout path to ESCALATED_TIMEOUT. An approval in the observed DRY_RUN mode records the simulated result and audit trail. Any blocklist entry is internal. External mail/firewall enforcement is outside this deployment. Component boundaries PhishGuardEdge protects traffic through CloudFront. The signed upload goes directly to S3. Lambda uses AWS-managed networking in this SAM template. The region and the service groups indicate placement and responsibility. QR extraction reads a URL locally, strips query and fragment for display, and supplies an indicator to Triage. PrepareAndWaitApproval uses lambda:invoke.waitForTaskToken: PrepareApproval saves the token, publishes to SNS and returns, while the Task waits up to 48 hours. The Wait for approval box is not a separate Wait state. In DRY_RUN, an APPROVED_DRY_RUN entry is not treated as a confirmed IOC when scoring later reports.
Score, assessment and workflow risk_score counts rule points. At 50 or above, assessment is SUSPICIOUS. Below that threshold the policy records UNKNOWN, with reason UNVERIFIED_URL or INSUFFICIENT_SIGNALS, and routes to NO_ACTION. Historical scores without an assessment display UNKNOWN / LEGACY. Poor input quality goes to NEEDS_MORE_INFO before scoring. Compare three cases.

title: Is S3 data safe once Block Public Access is enabled?
content:
A team keeps its reports in a private S3 bucket. One of its applications has permission to read them. If someone obtains that application’s credentials, what would let the team discover which reports were read? I used this question to look at three different jobs in S3 security.
Limit access. S3 Block Public Access guards against public access granted by policies and ACLs. A role with effective permission to call s3:GetObject can still read objects in scope. I would start by listing the prefixes each role needs to read and checking whether its policy grants access beyond them. Record object activity. I would enable CloudTrail S3 data events for reads on the reports bucket. This makes it possible to look up the principal, time and object associated with a GetObject request. A trail records these object-level events when you explicitly select them. Notify someone who can investigate. GuardDuty S3 Protection can flag unusual access. An EventBridge rule can route relevant findings to an SNS topic with a confirmed email subscription. GuardDuty can analyse S3 activity independently of the trail I configure for my own audit records. To exercise the notification path, I would use a GuardDuty sample finding that matches the rule and check whether the email arrives. That verifies delivery. To investigate a real alert, I would then consult the object-level history for the affected bucket.

title: AWS Cloud & AI Day Hanoi 2026
content:
When: 29 September 2026, 09:00–17:00 (Vietnam time)
Venue: Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City Role: Attendee
Taking an AI application beyond a demo I came to the event with a security question. Once an AI application can call tools on someone’s behalf, how can an operator establish what data it used, what it was allowed to do and who was responsible for the outcome? Dr. Werner Vogels’ keynote and contributions from Eric Yeo, Mai Le and Dr. Jens Lottner put that question in the context of enterprise modernisation. Examples from Katalon and Vietnamese financial institutions made me think about the people who inherit an application after the demo.
Three ideas I took away Repeatable deployment. The sessions on GitOps and internal developer platforms showed why teams invest in a standard route to production. With configuration in version control, an operator can look up who made a change and how it was reviewed. Workload identity. The IAM and AWS STS discussions connected the lifetime of a session to the permissions it carries. When an agent reads data or calls a tool, an operator needs to be able to trace the action to the identity that performed it. Answer quality. Latency and error rates help establish whether an application is serving traffic. For AI, I would also want to know which sources support an answer, whether the output exposes sensitive data and how many tokens the request consumed. A connection to PhishGuard When presenting one incident, I can show the cited playbook passage, explain which policy rule proposed the action and identify who approved it. Together, those details let a reviewer trace the evidence behind the explanation, the basis for the decision and the record left afterwards.

title: 2. Project proposal
content:
PhishGuard AI · Omnichannel phishing triage with human approval
Proposed pilot: an internal security operations team and employees reporting suspicious messages. Deployment region: US East (N. Virginia). The demo runs containment in DRY_RUN.
The operational problem An employee forwards a suspicious message to a general mailbox. A second employee reports an image of the same campaign. The analyst needs to identify each reporter, preserve precisely what each person submitted, explain a recommendation and find the decision later. Copying text into a chatbot helps with interpretation. Someone still has to connect the evidence, access controls, reviewer and outcome.
What the pilot delivers A Cognito-authenticated portal accepts pasted text, screenshots and EML files. An SES receiving rule accepts forwarded email from verified reporters. Ingest gives each report an incident ID and preserves a version of the original. Analysts use a redacted copy for routine work. A separate, audited request gives a privileged analyst short-lived access to the original.
The policy engine computes the score from indicators and named rules. Bedrock can retrieve playbooks and explain the result. If generation fails, the analyst still sees the rule result and the fallback reason. Where an action is proposed, Step Functions records a deadline, notifies SecOps and resumes only on a valid decision or a timeout. Approval records retain the human decision. A simulated block, a confirmed entry in the internal list and enforcement by an external product have different operational effects. External enforcement is outside the pilot.
Deliverables and acceptance Milestone Deliverable How to accept it Intake and preservation Portal, SES and separate evidence stores Submit a UTF-8 message and an image, then trace an incident to its S3 version. Repeating the same reporter request returns its incident. Analysis OCR, PII masking, policy evaluation and grounded summary Inspect the extracted Vietnamese text, triggered rules and evidence. Low-quality input asks for more information. Record the actual synthesis status. Approval Admin decision, callback and audit log An approved demo produces an audit record. An unanswered request expires. A late decision returns HTTP 409. Operations and handover Role-specific reads, alarms, workshop and cost model A second reporter cannot read the first reporter’s incident. Demonstrate alarm targets, a reproducible deployment and the assumptions behind cost. Boundaries and risks Object Lock Governance protects a raw version for seven days subject to authorized bypass. OCR may miss accents and masking can leave names or addresses. Forwarded headers describe the original message as supplied by the employee. SES authentication proves facts about the outer delivery. Analysts must interpret those separately. False-positive and false-negative rates on unseen real-world messages still require a labelled evaluation set.
Deployed scope. The CloudFront distribution has the PhishGuardEdge web ACL. Raw uploads go directly to S3. Image extraction supports Vietnamese/English OCR and URL QR codes. Six source playbooks support retrieval. Triage proposes eligible actions and Bedrock explains them.
Costs and pilot decision For a 30-day month with 300 reports, 90 images and 60 inbound emails, the model estimates USD 9.37, including the permanent WAF rules and one hosted zone. The Cost Explorer report for 1–23 November 2026 rounds to USD 0.00 within its export scope. Before extending the pilot, compare time to triage, false alerts, missed cases and manual review against the current mailbox process using an independently labelled set.

title: 5.2 · Prerequisites
content:
Use a lab account you are authorized to manage and select US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1. Some Lambda, table, user-pool-group and IAM-role names are fixed in the template. If the account already contains PhishGuard, start by inspecting the existing stack. Use a separate lab account for an independent deployment from scratch.
Install Git, Python 3.12 x64, Node.js 22 LTS, AWS CLI v2 and AWS SAM CLI. Docker is needed only for Linux container builds. The deploying identity needs stack management, S3 packaging and resource deployment permissions, including permission to pass the appropriate service roles. title: AWS KMS and envelope encryption: Who can read an encrypted S3 object?
content:
Why can a user download a readable PDF even though the S3 object is encrypted with AWS KMS? I followed a single upload and download to see where encryption ends and access control takes over.
On upload, in the basic SSE-KMS flow, S3 asks KMS for a data key. S3 encrypts the file with the plaintext data key, discards its plaintext copy and stores the encrypted copy of the key with the object. On download, an authorised read allows S3 to recover the data key and return the file contents. For that read I would review both the caller’s s3:GetObject permission and the effective permission to use kms:Decrypt on the key.
What changes when I enable S3 Bucket Keys? Consider a policy that checks kms:EncryptionContext:aws:s3:arn for a report in example-documents. The value S3 supplies by default depends on how the object was encrypted.
SSE-KMS configuration for the object Default ARN in the encryption context Without an S3 Bucket Key arn:aws:s3:::example-documents/reports/quarterly.pdf With an S3 Bucket Key arn:aws:s3:::example-documents S3 Bucket Keys reduce calls to KMS. A condition that expects the full object ARN can consequently fail to match. Before enabling Bucket Keys, I would review policies that use the encryption context and check where the team records individual reads. With fewer KMS events and a bucket-level ARN, S3 object-level data events matter for that investigation.

title: Does SQS FIFO guarantee exactly-once processing?
content:
Imagine Lambda receives evt-987 for order 1042, writes it to DynamoDB, then times out before the invocation completes. After the visibility timeout, the same message can become available again. What happens to the order on the second attempt?
At the queue, a FIFO queue preserves order within each MessageGroupId. If the producer retries with the same MessageDeduplicationId within five minutes, SQS suppresses the duplicate send. In this example the producer only sent one message. The second attempt comes from processing that existing message again.
At the database, if the whole operation consists of creating one item per event, I can use eventId as the partition key and give PutItem the condition attribute_not_exists(eventId). The first write creates the item. On a retry of the same event, the condition fails and the original item stays intact. A separate payment or email needs its own way to recognise a retry.
At the batch level, with partial batch responses enabled, AWS recommends stopping at the first failure for a FIFO queue and reporting both the failed and the unprocessed messages. A FIFO dead-letter queue can isolate repeated failures. Moving a message aside can change the order in which the business eventually completes the work.
The design question I would ask is concrete: if the function stops immediately after its first successful write, what will the next invocation do to order 1042?

title: 5.6 · Well-Architected review
content:
This section reviews how PhishGuard is operated, the reasons behind its design choices and the remaining limitations. During an investigation, the portal incident, its Step Functions execution and the S3 evidence version provide complementary views. The incident ID connects them.
Comparing the architecture with the configuration CloudFront serves the portal from S3 and routes /api/* to the HTTP API. WAF is associated with the distribution. Web and SES submissions converge at Ingest, which stores the original evidence before starting the workflow. Lambda uses AWS-managed networking; the template defines no application subnets.
Within the workflow, PrepareAndWaitApproval is a Task using lambda:invoke.waitForTaskToken. PrepareApproval stores the token, sends the notification and returns. The Task continues waiting for a callback, with a default timeout of 48 hours. The Prepare approval and Wait for approval boxes in the diagram describe two parts of this same mechanism.
AWS Well-Architected design decisions Pillar Application in PhishGuard Results and limitations Operational Excellence SAM deploys the backend; change sets expose the impact of an update. Two alarms monitor workflow failures and messages in the DLQ, with SNS notification actions. The image in 5.5.1 shows OK alarms with actions enabled at capture time. An actual alarm transition and its corresponding notification have not been demonstrated. Security JWTs and Cognito groups control API access. Raw evidence is isolated, with SSE-KMS, versioning and seven-day Governance retention. Admin API checks permissions before issuing raw access or accepting a decision. H02/H15 describe authorization checks. An appropriately authorized identity can bypass Governance. Pattern-based PII masking can miss names, addresses and OCR errors. Reliability Conditional writes and incident-named executions support retries. Asynchronous Ingest has a DLQ. The workflow has an approval timeout, and synthesis has a fallback. H04 and the partial-failure portion of H13 use local simulation. H14 has an expired-approval screenshot and a 409 response. Region-wide recovery objectives, RTO and RPO, have not been measured. Performance Efficiency Direct S3 uploads reduce data passing through the API. ExtractRedact uses x86_64, 512 MiB and OCR/QR layers. The callback does not keep a Lambda invocation running while a person decides. No p50/p95 benchmark is available. Measure image and text workloads separately using Duration, Billed Duration, Max Memory Used and Throttles. Cost Optimization Estimates use report counts, image volume, tokens and fixed service charges. Intake has a lifecycle policy, and logs have retention settings. 5.7 separates the budget, Calculator export and Cost Explorer data. WAF dominates the low-volume estimate; actual project-specific charges remain incompletely reconciled. Sustainability Event-driven processing avoids an application server waiting continuously for work. Temporary data has a retention limit. Cleanup must also account for old object versions. The project has no energy-use or emissions measurement. Handling a message in the DLQ Identify the alarm time and find the Ingest failure in CloudWatch Logs. Check that the input object still exists, verify read/write permissions and inspect any saved evidence version. Look up the DynamoDB incident and the execution with the same name to determine whether the workflow has started. Fix the cause and retry with lab data. Compare incident counts, raw versions and executions to detect duplicate processing. Intake has a three-day lifecycle. A message left in the DLQ for longer may reference an expired input object. Determine which data can still be recovered before replaying the event.
Protection boundaries of the lab WAF filters requests through CloudFront. Direct S3 uploads are controlled by the presigned policy and Ingest; incoming email passes through SES. The template retains the HTTP API’s execute-api endpoint and does not require every API call to pass through CloudFront. JWT checks, authorization and API throttling still apply to direct calls.
The Cognito template sets MFA to OFF. Raw-evidence auditing records issuance of a 60-second URL, rather than proving an object download. These areas need further assessment before using real data or deploying for an organization. Containment currently simulates an action or updates an internal list; it does not modify a firewall or email gateway.

title: 6. Self-assessment
content:
In my first IAM, VPC and EC2 labs, a successful connection to an instance usually marked the end of the exercise for me. Monitoring, automation and security labs changed that habit. I started asking who could perform the operation, where its result appeared and whether another person could reproduce it. That change is the clearest sign of progress I see in my FCAJ worklog.
Self-assessment I based these ratings on lab notes, technical writing, events and project evidence available by 24 November 2026. I gave myself a Good rating where most of my experience still comes from individual exercises.
No. Criterion Basis for my rating Very good Good Average 1 Technical knowledge I can explain how identity, networking, compute and storage fit together. I need more practice choosing between services when both traffic and budget change. ✓ 2 Ability to learn I moved from console exercises to using the CLI, reading templates and checking the resulting deployment. ✓ 3 Initiative When a lab behaves differently from its instructions, I consult the documentation and change one setting at a time. ✓ 4 Responsibility I keep evidence for reported results and identify checks that my account permissions leave open. ✓ 5 Discipline and time management Weekly entries help me track progress. Some image captions and cost reconciliation still accumulated near the deadline. ✓ 6 Response to feedback Feedback on the diagram and navigation led me to retrace data flows and organize instructions around the reader’s tasks. ✓ 7 Communication Writing in Vietnamese and English improved my use of technical terms. My spoken explanations sometimes include more detail than the listener needs. ✓ 8 Collaboration I can prepare a reproducible example for discussion. Most of my evidence comes from individual labs, and I would benefit from paired deployments. ✓ 9 Professional conduct I pay attention to account scope, permissions and information visible in screenshots used for handover. ✓ 10 Problem solving During a rollback I traced a failed resource to the denied IAM action and distinguished it from updates cancelled as a consequence. ✓ 11 Project contribution I brought together security, monitoring and infrastructure-as-code exercises in a workshop that another learner can deploy, verify and clean up. ✓ 12 Overall performance I can build and explain a lab system. Team delivery, performance measurement and longer-term operations remain development areas. ✓ Strengths I learn well when I have a result I can inspect. At first a monitoring graph with a single point looked incomplete. Comparing the request time, the rule dimension and the statistic showed me how one point could answer the question I was testing. Writing technical blog posts exercises the same skill. Before explaining how a service behaves, I have to find an example a reader could check independently.
Systems Manager and infrastructure as code gave me another example. In the operations week I focused on carrying out a task consistently across resources. Reading a change set the following week moved my question earlier in the process: which resources would update in place and which might be replaced? Those exercises also changed the way I plan and hand over work.
Areas for improvement I sometimes spend so long getting one stage to work that my notes omit its starting configuration. Several days later that makes the result harder to explain. The AI and architecture events also showed me how much separates following a demonstration from choosing between two reasonable designs myself. I want to be able to name the deciding constraint, estimate its cost and say what would change my decision.
Improvement plan Before my next lab, I will record the goal, initial configuration and expected result. Afterwards I will document one failure and how I narrowed down its cause. Each week I will choose one design decision, write a short explanation in English and present it to a peer in three minutes. Their questions will show where my explanation needs work. On my next shared exercise I want to alternate between writing instructions and following someone else’s instructions in a fresh environment. I will use the reader’s observations to revise the handover. My overall self-rating at this stage is Good. The FCAJ habit I most want to keep is supporting what I have learned with a result someone else can verify.

title: 7. Sharing and feedback
content:
Overall feedback on the program 1. Learning environment and working format What I enjoyed about FCAJ was being able to start with a small question and answer it through a lab. In an early permissions exercise the question was simply which identity could open a resource. Later, when I used the CLI and deployed templates, I recognized that same question at almost every step. Independent practice gave me time to repeat a difficult exercise. In weeks with several labs, a short list of priorities would have helped me decide what to study in depth first.
2. Support from mentors and organizers The sharing sessions let me hear practitioners explain why they chose a particular design. That reasoning is difficult to get from a sequence of instructions alone. I found it easier to frame a question once I could state my goal, what I had tried and what I actually observed. A shared collection of recurring questions about regions, identities and permissions would give beginners a useful first check and leave more discussion time for difficult cases.
3. Relevance of the curriculum As an Information Assurance student, I found the progression from identity and networking to storage, monitoring and security especially useful. Knowing how to find a log made the incident-response material easier to follow. Migration, hybrid environments and containers also exposed me to more than one way of moving an application to the cloud. I would welcome a short exercise at each transition that calls on a skill from the previous topic.
4. Opportunities to develop technical skills The biggest lesson for me was how much there is to do after a service first responds. Infrastructure as code gave me a way to inspect a proposed change. Monitoring required me to select a meaningful metric. Cost analysis required me to define the billing period and workload before interpreting a number. Sessions on AI and retrieval also gave me a new question to ask of an application: which source document supports its answer?
After the Docker, ECS and EKS labs, I would have welcomed a discussion of the same application running on containers or Lambda. Asking each learner to choose a deployment and defend it in terms of traffic, updates and running costs would bring the two topics together.
5. Teamwork and reporting Keeping a weekly worklog exposed entries where I had recorded clicks without explaining the result. Writing bilingual blog posts made me consider someone who had never run the lab. I would enjoy a workshop exchange where one student follows another’s instructions in a fresh environment while the author observes. Seeing where the reader stops would reveal assumptions that are almost invisible to the person who wrote the guide.
6. Participation requirements and practical arrangements For a student managing an AWS account, knowing what may continue to incur charges after a session is important. Clear prerequisites make a lab much easier to plan. A short note at the beginning listing the target region, permissions, indicative cost and resources needed for the following session would make that planning easier still.
Further questions What was most satisfying? I could see the same skill develop over time. Early on I read logs to fix a lab. Later I used logs and execution times to explain to another reader why a request reached a particular outcome. That change made my progress visible.
What would help future participants? I would add a short self-check at the end of each stage, with a sample input, one common failure and an expected result. A learner could then decide whether to move on or revisit a particular topic.
Would I recommend FCAJ to a friend? Yes, especially to someone curious about the day-to-day work of a cloud engineer. I would suggest setting aside time for notes and cleanup within each session. Both are easy to postpone as soon as the lab starts working.
Suggestions and hopes for the future For the program. I would set aside one short peer design review. Each student would explain a decision, describe a failure the design anticipates and take a question from a peer. Continuing involvement. I hope to join more sessions on cloud security, multi-account governance and incident investigation. I would also like to write a short lab that a future participant can reproduce in their own account. A closing note. I appreciate the opportunity FCAJ gives students to try the actual work involved in running cloud systems. The habit I will take with me is keeping enough evidence to explain a technical decision to someone else. Weekly worklog · Technical blog posts · Events attended

title: 5.8 · Clean up resources
content: Begin cleanup only when no one still needs the demo environment. Export test results, the estimate and billing data. Inventory resources in the application stack, KB stack and outside CloudFormation. Stop new submissions, review executions waiting for approval and handle them according to the lab’s policy. Remove only the lab’s SES receipt rule. If DNS or a domain is shared, preserve MX records and rules used by other email workloads. Remove CloudFront resource associations as appropriate, disable the distribution, wait for Deployed, then delete it when ready. Check any flat-rate subscription, standalone WAF/web ACL and recurring charges. Unsubscribe demo email addresses if the SNS topic is retained. Delete data sources and the KB before their vector-storage resources. Review resources with Retain or RetainExceptOnCreate, including tables, buckets, keys and the user pool. For versioned S3 buckets, check versions and delete markers. Keep evidence for its committed retention period, then remove it using the agreed lab procedure. Review CloudFormation, S3, S3 Vectors, Bedrock Guardrails, IAM roles, Cognito domains, CloudWatch logs/alarms, SQS, SNS, Route 53, Budgets and any dedicated SAM artifact bucket. Schedule KMS key deletion only after identifying data that still needs decryption. Recheck Bills/Cost Explorer after data updates, including automatic domain renewal if a domain was purchased for the lab. For the separate edge stack, disassociate the web ACL from its distribution before deleting the ACL and stack. Record each retained resource, its owner and the next date for reviewing its charges.
